learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements Explained
learn.intro: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are the backbone of renewable energy financing. They allow developers to secure long-term buyers for clean electricity, reducing financial risk and enabling large-scale projects to move forward. Understanding PPAs helps investors, corporations, and policymakers accelerate the shift to sustainable energy systems.
learn.c1_text: A Power Purchase Agreement is a long-term contract between an electricity generator and a buyer. Think of it like a decade-long subscription for clean energy. The generator promises to deliver a set amount of power at a fixed price, while the buyer agrees to purchase it. This stability attracts investors who might otherwise avoid volatile energy markets.
learn.c2_text: PPAs provide predictable revenue streams that banks use to approve construction loans. With a signed agreement, developers can secure up to 70% debt financing at lower interest rates. This reduces upfront capital needs and makes solar or wind farms financially viable without heavy government subsidies.
learn.c3_text: India has leveraged PPAs to attract over $15 billion in renewable energy investments since 2014. The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) auctions long-term PPAs, enabling projects like the 2,250 MW Bhadla Solar Park. These agreements have helped India reach 90 GW of renewable capacity by 2024.
learn.stat2: Corporate PPAs globally reached 7.7 GW in 2020
learn.stat4: Up to 70% of project costs can be debt-financed via PPAs

learn.title: Electric Vehicles: Motors and Charging
learn.intro: Electric vehicles are transforming transportation by replacing internal combustion engines with efficient electric motors. Understanding how they work—from regenerative braking to charging infrastructure—is key to appreciating their role in decarbonizing mobility and reducing urban air pollution worldwide.
learn.c1_text: Unlike gasoline engines with hundreds of moving parts, electric motors have just one: a rotating shaft. Powered by batteries, they convert electrical energy directly into motion. A typical EV motor delivers full torque instantly, meaning rapid acceleration from a standstill—often quicker than sports cars.
learn.c2_text: When you lift your foot off the accelerator, regenerative braking kicks in. Instead of wasting kinetic energy as heat through traditional brakes, the motor runs backward, acting as a generator. This recaptures up to 30% of energy normally lost, extending driving range by several kilometers per stop.
learn.c3_text: India launched the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme with ₹1,000 crore allocation. As of 2024, over 500,000 EVs are registered, supported by 12,000+ charging points. The government aims for 30% vehicle electrification by 2030.
learn.stat1: EVs have 1 moving part vs 200+ in gasoline engines
learn.stat2: Regenerative braking recaptures up to 30% of energy
learn.stat4: Over 12,000 charging points installed in India (2024)

learn.title: Solar PV and the Photoelectric Effect
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect—a phenomenon that won Einstein his Nobel Prize. This clean, silent technology powers everything from rooftop homes to massive solar farms, making it central to global renewable energy expansion.
learn.c1_text: When photons from sunlight strike a solar cell, they knock electrons loose from their atoms. This is the photoelectric effect. The freed electrons flow through circuits as direct current (DC) electricity. It's like raindrops knocking marbles off a table—each photon dislodges an electron to generate power.
learn.c2_text: Solar panels produce DC electricity, but homes and grids use alternating current (AC). An inverter converts DC to AC, syncing with grid frequency. Modern inverters achieve over 98% efficiency. Excess power feeds back into the grid or charges battery storage systems for later use.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 3rd globally in solar capacity with 90 GW installed by 2024. The International Solar Alliance, co-founded by India, aims to mobilize $1 trillion in solar investment. Projects like Bhadla Solar Park—one of the world's largest—showcase India's commitment to scaling solar rapidly.
learn.stat2: Solar panels can last 25-30 years with minimal degradation
learn.stat4: Bhadla Solar Park spans 14,000 acres in Rajasthan

learn.title: Wind Turbine Lifespan and Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbines are engineered to last 20-25 years, but their fiberglass blades pose recycling challenges at end-of-life. As the global wind fleet ages, sustainable disposal and reuse strategies are critical to maintaining wind energy's environmental benefits and supporting circular economy principles.
learn.c1_text: Most wind turbines operate for 20-25 years under normal conditions. Key factors include material fatigue, weather exposure, and maintenance quality. Onshore turbines face fewer environmental stresses than offshore units, which deal with salt corrosion and higher wind loads but often justify longer operational periods due to consistent wind resources.
learn.c2_text: Turbine blades are made of composite materials that are difficult to separate. Traditional methods involve shredding for cement production or landfilling. New techniques include mechanical recycling, chemical depolymerization, and repurposing blades for construction materials. Some companies now create playground equipment and park benches from old blades.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 4th globally in wind capacity with 45 GW installed by 2024. The National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy promotes hybrid projects. Tamil Nadu leads with 13 GW capacity. As early turbines reach end-of-life around 2030, India is developing blade recycling facilities to manage the transition sustainably.
learn.stat3: Over 450 million tons of blade material expected to retire globally by 2050
learn.stat4: Tamil Nadu accounts for 30% of India's wind capacity

learn.title: Production Linked Incentive for Solar Manufacturing
learn.intro: India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme aims to boost domestic solar manufacturing and reduce import dependence. By incentivizing local production of high-efficiency solar modules, the policy supports India's renewable energy targets while strengthening supply chain resilience and creating green jobs.
learn.c1_text: The PLI scheme provides financial incentives to manufacturers based on sales volume of goods manufactured in India. For solar, it offers 6-12 paise/kWh benefit for five years. This makes domestic production competitive against imports, particularly from China which dominates 80% of global solar manufacturing.
learn.c2_text: The scheme targets 60 GW of integrated solar manufacturing capacity, including polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells, and modules. Five mega projects were approved with total investment of ₹19,500 crore. This vertical integration reduces supply chain risks and positions India as a global solar manufacturing hub.
learn.c3_text: By 2024, the PLI scheme attracted investments worth ₹43,000 crore in solar manufacturing. Reliance Industries plans a $10 billion green energy complex in Gujarat. The initiative supports India's goal of 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030 while reducing reliance on Chinese imports for critical components.

learn.stat2: 5 mega solar manufacturing projects approved with ₹19,500 crore investment
learn.stat3: China dominates 80% of global solar manufacturing

learn.title: Floating Solar Farms and Water Conservation
learn.intro: Floating solar farms installed on reservoirs and lakes generate clean electricity while conserving water through reduced evaporation. This innovative approach maximizes land use efficiency, especially in densely populated areas, and offers dual environmental benefits that make it attractive for sustainable development.
learn.c1_text: Floating solar panels are mounted on pontoons and anchored to the seabed or lake bed. They generate electricity just like land-based panels but benefit from cooling effects of water, increasing efficiency by 5-10%. The installation also reduces algae growth and inhibits water evaporation significantly.
learn.c2_text: A 1 MW floating solar array can save approximately 2.5 million liters of water annually through reduced evaporation. In drought-prone regions, this is equivalent to supplying water to 1,000 households. The panels also improve water quality by limiting sunlight penetration and reducing temperature fluctuations.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 92,000 sq km of water bodies suitable for floating solar. The 600 MW Ramagundam project in Telangana is among the largest. The government targets 10 GW of floating solar capacity by 2030. NTPC's 120 MW Kayamkulam project demonstrates successful integration with existing hydroelectric infrastructure.

learn.stat2: Floating solar improves panel efficiency by 5-10% due to cooling
learn.stat3: 1 MW floating array saves 2.5 million liters of water annually
learn.stat4: India identified 92,000 sq km of water bodies for floating solar potential
